messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.
38 mm motor max. I'm L1, so H and I motors. Looking for roughly 1,400 ft. Winds are typically 10 mph. Show me what you've got.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: motor diameter is a maximum of 38 mm. The flyer is Level 1, so the motor is an H or an I (fixed class band). Apogee roughly 1,400 ft. 1400 * 0.3048 = 427 m, within about 5%. Wind is typically 10 mph: 10 * 0.447 = 4.47 m/s, passed on every flight. Landing limit not stated, so 6 m/s. Rail 1.5 m, vertical, sea level, single stage, one chute.
2. Feasibility: 427 m with no drag needs sqrt(2 * 9.81 * 427) = 92 m/s. That is a small H on a normal airframe. An I will only stay that low if the rocket is heavy or draggy, which is a poor use of the motor. Looking up a few 29 mm and 38 mm H motors.

2. Feasibility: H165R is class H, 160.9 N*s, 158.5 N, burn 1.01 s, 29 mm, delays 10 and 14 s. H128W is similar impulse but only a 14 s delay. H180W is 233.7 N*s with only a 6 s delay, more likely to open early and to fly past 427 m. All three are under the 38 mm cap. H165R-10 is the closest match. In a 4.47 m/s wind I want a 66 mm tube, not a minimum-diameter dart.
3. Size: guessed liftoff mass 0.60 kg. Thrust-to-weight = 158.5 / (0.60 * 9.81) = 26.9. Rail acceleration (158.5 - 5.89) / 0.60 = 254 m/s^2, exit speed sqrt(2 * 254 * 1.5) = 27.6 m/s. Descent mass 0.60 - 0.091 = 0.509 kg. At 5 m/s and Cd 0.8, area = 2 * 0.509 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 5^2) = 0.408 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 0.408 / 3.1416) = 0.721 m. A 0.80 m chute stays under 6 m/s. Burnout at 1.01 s plus the 10 s delay ejects near 11 s.
4. Draft: 66 mm blue tube, 0.65 m long, fiberglass ogive, three basswood fins, 29 mm mount, H165R-10, 0.80 m chute. Wind 4.47 m/s.

4. Check: the simulator gives 786.8 m. Against 427 m that is (786.8 - 427) / 427 = 0.843, about 84% high. Margin is 0.78 cal, under 1.0, and 0.78 cal through the burn. Landing 5.0 m/s is under 6. Rail exit 26.5 m/s, thrust-to-weight 22.2. The chute opens at 11.1 s, right on apogee. Liftoff mass 0.729 kg is heavier than my 0.60 kg guess and it still flew high, so mass is not the main knob. Motor is the 29 mm H165R, legal for L1 and under 38 mm.
5. Fix: 786.8 m is the miss that matters, and a wider tube is the drag change. Nose and body go from 0.066 m to 0.102 m, a 4 inch airframe. Reference diameter grows, so the margin will fall from 0.78 cal and will need another look. Fins, motor and chute stay. Wall thickness stays 0.0018 m, so the mount still fits.

4. Check: the simulator gives a margin of -0.1 cal. The 4 inch tube made the old fins tiny, and the rocket is unstable. Apogee came down to 530.0 m, still high: (530.0 - 427) / 427 = 0.241, about 24% over the 5% band. Landing is 6.0 m/s, right on the 6 m/s limit. Rail exit 22.1 m/s, thrust-to-weight 16.1. The chute opens at 11.1 s, after apogee at 9.48 s.
5. Fix: -0.1 cal is the failure I have to clear before the altitude number means anything. Fin span goes from 0.07 m to 0.15 m, root from 0.12 m to 0.18 m, tip from 0.05 m to 0.075 m, sweep 0.09 m. Area goes from (0.12 + 0.05) / 2 * 0.07 = 0.0060 m^2 to (0.18 + 0.075) / 2 * 0.15 = 0.0191 m^2. The extra fin drag should also pull 530 m down some. Tube, motor and chute stay. Landing is already at 6.0 m/s, so I will watch it.

5. Fix: 0.99 cal and 450.3 m need a little more nose mass, and 6.4 m/s needs a bigger chute. One knob cannot do both, because nose mass makes the landing faster. Nose weight goes from 0.05 kg to 0.08 kg, and the chute goes from 0.80 m to 1.05 m. Landing speed scales about inversely with diameter, so 6.4 * 0.80 / 1.05 = 4.9 m/s before the extra mass, with a little of that given back. The last 0.05 kg dropped apogee by 462.5 - 450.3 = 12.2 m, so another 0.03 kg should take 450 m under the 5% ceiling and the margin through 1 cal.

Landing is 5.1 m/s, under 6. Rail exit 20.2 m/s, thrust-to-weight 13.6. Motor is the 29 mm H165R, which is an H and under the 38 mm cap. The chute still opens at 11.1 s, after apogee at 8.88 s, and the tool warns of a 21.2 m/s opening. That is not a gate, and the 10 s delay is the shortest this motor has.
5. Fix: no further change; altitude, margin and landing all pass.
6. Uncertainty: 435.9 m is inside the band but not in the middle. A lighter build, or less of the 0.08 kg nose weight, climbs back over the top. The 1.1 cal margin is thin for a 4.47 m/s wind, so it will weathercock. The opening at 21.2 m/s is hard on the nylon; an electronic chute at apogee would be kinder, and it would not change the altitude because the motor already burns out well before apogee. Drift was 286 m.
